topics.title: Atomic number, mass, shells and quantum numbers

questions.text: Which statements best characterize the focus of physical metallurgy?

statements.text: It studies physical and mechanical characteristics of metals and alloys.
It examines how composition, mechanical processing and heat treatment influence those characteristics.
Microstructure–property relationships are central to the subject.
After heat treatment, property changes are attributed mainly to changes in bulk composition; microstructure and defect structure are secondary.

questions.keyExplanation: Statements 1–3 describe the scope of physical metallurgy. Statement 4 is incorrect because heat treatment commonly changes phase distribution, grain structure, precipitates and defect populations without changing the alloy's bulk composition.
questions.concise: Physical metallurgy links composition and processing to microstructure and properties; heat treatment need not change bulk composition.
questions.detailed: Physical metallurgy investigates how processing and composition create microstructures that control material properties. A heat treatment can change phases, grain size, precipitate distribution and dislocation density while leaving the nominal bulk composition essentially unchanged. Therefore statement 4 reverses the usual microstructure-based explanation.

questions.text: The atomic number Z of an element is defined as the number of:
questions.keyExplanation: Z = number of protons ( = electrons in a neutral atom). This is what defines the element.
questions.concise: Atomic number Z counts protons.
questions.detailed: The atomic number Z is the number of protons in the nucleus, so **(c)** is correct. Option (a) gives the neutron count; (b) gives the mass number (protons plus neutrons); and (d) refers to outer-shell electrons.

questions.text: The maximum number of electrons that the *n* = 3 shell can accommodate is:
questions.detailed: The maximum number of electrons in shell n = 3 is 2n² = 2 × 3² = 18, so **(c)** is correct. Option (a), 8, is the n = 2 shell capacity; (b), 24, is not the capacity; and (d), 32, is the n = 4 capacity.

questions.text: The first four shells hold a maximum of, respectively:
questions.detailed: Using 2n², the first four shell capacities are 2, 8, 18 and 32. **(a)** is correct. Option (b) incorrectly gives 16 for the third shell; (c) is the s, p, d, f subshell-capacity sequence; and (d) incorrectly gives 36 for the fourth shell.

questions.text: The subshell designated by the azimuthal quantum number *l* = 2 is:
questions.keyExplanation: s, p, d, f correspond to l = 0, 1, 2, 3.
questions.concise: l = 2 is the d subshell.
questions.detailed:
The azimuthal quantum number l labels subshell *shape*:
```
l = 0 → s
l = 1 → p
l = 2 → d
l = 3 → f
```
So l = 2 → d. This mapping is worth memorising cold; it recurs in transition-metal chemistry.

questions.text: Match the quantum number to what it fixes.
questions.keyExplanation: n→shell energy, l→subshell shape, mₗ→orientation, mₛ→spin.
questions.concise: n→shell energy, l→subshell shape, mₗ→orientation, mₛ→spin.
questions.detailed:
| Quantum number | Symbol | What it fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Principal | n | overall shell energy and size |
| Azimuthal | l | subshell shape (s, p, d, f) |
| Magnetic | mₗ | orbital orientation in space |
| Spin | mₛ | electron spin direction (±½) |

Option (a) is the only one placing all four correctly. The distractors shuffle mₗ and mₛ,
which is the commonest mix-up since both have "m" in their names.

questions.text: The Pauli exclusion principle permits a maximum of two electrons in the same quantum state, and they must have opposite spin.
questions.keyExplanation: Pauli: max two electrons of opposite spin per quantum state.
questions.concise: Pauli exclusion principle — max 2 electrons of opposite spin per quantum state.
questions.detailed:
No two electrons in an atom can share the same set of four quantum numbers.
The only way to have two electrons "together" is for their spins to be opposite (+½ and −½).
This is exactly what allows the shell capacity to be 2n² rather than n² — each of the n²
orbital states holds 2 spin-antiparallel electrons.

questions.text: The one important exception to simple "fill from the inside out" shell filling is:
questions.keyExplanation: 4s fills before 3d — the wrinkle that makes transition metals behave as they do.
questions.concise: The 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d when filling from an empty atom.
questions.detailed: The 4s subshell fills before 3d in the usual neutral-atom filling sequence, so **(d)** is correct. Option (a) reverses this order; (b) is not the relevant 4s/3d exception; and (c) is an unrelated ordering.

questions.text: Why is the 4s-before-3d exception worth remembering for the rest of a metallurgy course?

statements.text: It is why transition metals (Fe, Ti, Cr, Mn) behave as they do.
It explains why transition metals have variable valence.
It is the reason transition metals form interstitial compounds with carbon and nitrogen.
It determines the atomic mass of iron.

questions.keyExplanation: It explains transition-metal chemistry/valence. It does **not** cause interstitial carbide formation (item 3 is a bonding/size effect) nor determine atomic mass (item 4).
questions.concise: The 4s/3d exception explains transition-metal behaviour and variable valence; it does not cause interstitial carbide formation or determine atomic mass.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: it is the origin of transition-metal chemistry.
- Item 2 — TRUE: because 4s and 3d are close in energy, transition metals can lose varying
  numbers of electrons → variable valence (e.g. Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺).
- Item 3 — FALSE: interstitial compound formation (Fe₃C, TiC) is a *size and bonding* effect —
  the small non-metal fits an interstice — not a shell-filling effect.
- Item 4 — FALSE: atomic mass is set by protons + neutrons, unrelated to orbital order.

questions.text: Match the element class to its members.
tableRows: (i) B, Ge, Si, Sb, As, Te, Po
(ii) N, O, P, S and the noble gases
questions.keyExplanation: Metals ≈ ¾ of elements; metalloids = B, Ge, Si, Sb, As, Te, Po; non-metals = N, O, P, S + noble gases.
questions.concise: Metals ≈ ¾ of elements; metalloids = B, Ge, Si, Sb, As, Te, Po; non-metals = N, O, P, S + noble gases.
questions.detailed: In BCC, atoms touch along the body diagonal, whose length √3a spans four atomic radii: √3a = 4R. **(a)** is correct. Option (b), the cube edge, and (c), the face diagonal, are not contact directions in BCC.

questions.text: Match the bond type to its mechanism.
questions.keyExplanation: Ionic = transfer; covalent = localised sharing; metallic = delocalised sharing; vdW = induced dipole.
questions.concise: Ionic=transfer, covalent=localised sharing, metallic=delocalised sharing, vdW=induced dipole.
questions.detailed: In FCC, atoms touch along a face diagonal, whose length √2a spans four atomic radii: √2a = 4R. **(c)** is correct. The cube edge (a) and body diagonal (b) are not the contact directions for FCC.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the *covalent* bond is/are correct?

statements.text: It is strongly directional.
It is non-directional.
Typical bond energy lies in the range 200–1000 kJ/mol.
Diamond (C) is a standard example.

questions.keyExplanation: Covalent bonds are directional (2 is false), 200–1000 kJ/mol, diamond is the classic example. [P1]
questions.concise: Covalent bonds are directional, 200–1000 kJ/mol; diamond is the classic example.
questions.detailed: For BCC, the body diagonal relation is √3a = 4R, so a = 4R/√3. **(d)** is correct. Option (a), 2R, is the simple-cubic edge relation; (b), 2√2R, is FCC; and (c), 4R/√2, is another form of the FCC relation.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are consequences of the *metallic* bond?

statements.text: High electrical and thermal conductivity.
Ductility, because ion cores can slide past one another without breaking a specific fixed bond.
Metallic luster and opacity.
Hardness and brittleness.

questions.keyExplanation: 1–3 are all metallic-bond consequences. Item 4 (hard & brittle) describes *ionic/covalent* solids. [P3] — the *ductility* arises from bonding, not from "heat".
questions.concise: Metallic bonding gives conductivity and ductility, not brittleness.
questions.detailed: For FCC, the face diagonal relation is √2a = 4R, so a = 4R/√2 = 2√2R. **(d)** is correct. Option (a), 2R, is simple cubic; (b), 4R/√3, is BCC; and (c), 4R, is not the FCC lattice parameter.

questions.assertion: Ionic solids are hard, brittle and electrical insulators.
questions.reason: In an ionic bond, electrons are transferred, producing a non-directional but charge-ordered arrangement that is disrupted when planes slip.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R is **not** the correct explanation

options.label: c
options.text: Both A and R true, R is the correct explanation of A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true and R correctly explains A: charge-ordering + slip disruption → brittleness.
questions.concise: Charge-ordered, non-directional bonding + slip disruption explains ionic hardness and brittleness.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: ionic solids (e.g. NaCl) are hard, brittle and insulating.
- R is TRUE: ionic bonding is electron transfer producing a charge-ordered arrangement; when
  planes try to slip, like-charged ions come into register and repel, so the crystal cleaves.

R correctly explains A — the brittleness is a direct consequence of the charge ordering that
also makes them hard. They are insulators because there are no free electrons (contrast Q18).

questions.text: Van der Waals forces best described as:

statements.text: a weak, secondary attraction between otherwise neutral atoms or molecules
significant mainly at low temperature, where thermal agitation does not swamp them
what holds solid noble gases (Ar, Ne) together
a primary bond of 600–1500 kJ/mol

questions.keyExplanation: vdW is weak (1–10 kJ/mol), so item 4 is false.
questions.concise: vdW is a weak (1–10 kJ/mol) secondary attraction; it holds solid Ar and Ne.
questions.detailed: At room temperature, aluminium is FCC, so **(d)** is correct. α-Fe, Cr and W are BCC. Do not confuse α-Fe (BCC) with γ-Fe (FCC).

questions.text: Increasing order of typical bond energy (kJ/mol) is:

options.label: a
options.text: metallic < ionic < covalent < van der Waals

options.label: b
options.text: van der Waals < metallic < covalent < ionic

options.label: c
options.text: van der Waals < covalent < ionic < metallic

options.label: d
options.text: ionic < covalent < metallic < van der Waals

questions.detailed: The n = 3 shell contains 3s, 3p and 3d subshells, with capacities 2 + 6 + 10 = 18. **(c)** is correct. Option (b), 24, is not the n = 3 shell capacity; (a) and (d) are capacities of other shells.

questions.text: Which statements correctly distinguish metallic bonding from covalent bonding?

statements.text: Metallic bonding uses delocalised valence electrons, whereas covalent bonding involves shared electron pairs localised between bonded atoms.
Metallic bonding is generally non-directional, whereas covalent bonding is directional.
Metallic bonds are always at least ten times weaker than covalent bonds.
The non-directional character of metallic bonding helps explain why many metals can deform plastically, while covalent network solids are often brittle.

questions.keyExplanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are broadly correct for the introductory comparison. Statement 3 is false because metallic and covalent bond energies overlap substantially; metallic bonding is not universally an order of magnitude weaker.
questions.concise: Metallic bonding is delocalised and non-directional; covalent bonding is directional. Their bond energies are not separated by a universal tenfold ratio.
questions.detailed: Metallic bonding is described using delocalised valence electrons and is generally non-directional, helping explain the plasticity of many metals. Covalent bonds are directional; covalent network solids such as diamond are often brittle. Bond-energy ranges overlap, so one cannot claim that metallic bonds are always at least ten times weaker than covalent bonds.

questions.text: In the metallic bond, valence electrons:

options.label: b
options.text: detach from individual atoms and form a shared, delocalised electron cloud

options.label: c
options.text: are transferred entirely to the nearest non-metal

questions.keyExplanation: Delocalised electron gas / "electron sea" around positive ion cores.
questions.concise: The valence electrons form a shared "electron sea" around the ion cores.
questions.detailed:
In metallic bonding the valence electrons detach from individual atoms and become
shared across the whole metal — a delocalised electron cloud (or "electron sea") of negative
charge surrounding a lattice of positive ion cores.
- (a) Electrons bound to individual atoms → that is covalent/ionic, not metallic.
- (c) Transferred entirely to the nearest non-metal → that is *ionic* bonding.
- (d) Localised in directional pairs → that is *covalent* bonding.
All four metallic properties (conductivity, ductility, luster, opacity) trace back to this
one structural fact of delocalisation.

questions.text: Metallic elements show all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: b
options.text: capacity for substantial plastic deformation before fracture

options.label: c
options.text: electrical insulation in the solid state

questions.keyExplanation: Metals are *conductors*, not insulators — the free-electron cloud carries charge.
questions.concise: Metals conduct electricity; they are the opposite of insulators.
questions.detailed: The EXCEPT item is **(c)**: metals are electrical conductors, not electrical insulators. Options (a), (b) and (d) are genuine metallic properties: high thermal conductivity, plastic deformability and reflectivity.

questions.assertion: Metals are ductile whereas ionic and covalent solids are brittle.
questions.reason: The metallic bond is non-directional and delocalised, so ion cores can be shifted past one another without breaking a specific fixed bond.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Non-directional delocalised bonding is exactly why metals deform without fracture.
questions.concise: Non-directional delocalised bonding is exactly why metals deform without fracture.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: metals are ductile; ionic and covalent solids are brittle.
- R is TRUE: the metallic bond is non-directional and delocalised, so ion cores can shift past
  one another without breaking a specific fixed bond.

R correctly explains A. Contrast with Q14 (ionic): there, slip *breaks* fixed charge-ordering;
here, slip *preserves* the bonding because it is non-directional. Same "slip" concept, opposite
outcome — that is the pair worth holding in your head.

questions.text: A certain solid has a primary bond energy of only 1–10 kJ/mol and exists as a noble gas at low temperature. It is bonded by:
questions.keyExplanation: 1–10 kJ/mol + noble gas ⇒ van der Waals.
questions.concise: 1–10 kJ/mol + noble gas at low temperature ⇒ van der Waals.
questions.detailed:
The two clues both point to vdW:
1. Bond energy of only 1–10 kJ/mol — the weakest class by far.
2. Exists as a noble gas at low temperature — Ar, Ne, etc. are held together only by induced
   dipole (vdW) attractions.
Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds are all "hundreds of kJ/mol" primary bonds, so they are
excluded on energy alone.

questions.text: The equilibrium interatomic spacing *r₀* corresponds to the point where:

options.label: a
options.text: the net force is zero and the net potential energy is a minimum

options.label: b
options.text: the attractive force is a maximum

options.label: d
options.text: the two atoms are in contact and touching

questions.keyExplanation: Net force zero ⟺ dE/dr = 0 ⟺ energy minimum at *r₀*.
questions.concise: At r₀, attraction balances repulsion → net force zero, energy minimum.
questions.detailed: At equilibrium spacing r₀, the net force is zero and the interatomic potential energy is at a minimum. **(a)** is correct. Option (b) incorrectly makes the attractive force maximal; (c) incorrectly sets the repulsive force to zero; and (d) treats atoms as hard spheres in literal contact.

questions.text: The depth of the interatomic energy well, *E₀*, is a measure of the:
questions.keyExplanation: Well depth *E₀* = bond energy; correlates with melting point.
questions.concise: The well depth E₀ measures bond energy (and correlates with melting point).
questions.detailed: The depth E₀ of the interatomic potential-energy well measures the bond energy required to separate the atoms. **(d)** is correct. Atomic radius is associated with the position r₀; coordination number and crystal structure are not measured by the well depth.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are correctly paired with the feature of the interatomic energy curve that produces it?

statements.text: Curvature (stiffness) of the well at *r₀* → elastic (Young's) modulus
Depth of the well → melting point and bond energy
Asymmetry of the well → thermal expansion
Position of *r₀* → coordination number

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. *r₀* gives atomic diameter, **not** coordination number (item 4 false). [P1]
questions.concise: Curvature→modulus, depth→melting/bond energy, asymmetry→thermal expansion; r₀ does *not* set coordination number.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: a stiffer (more curved) well at r₀ means a larger elastic (Young's) modulus.
- Item 2 — TRUE: well depth = bond energy, which correlates with melting point.
- Item 3 — TRUE: the *asymmetry* of the well is the origin of thermal expansion.
- Item 4 — FALSE: r₀ gives the atomic *diameter*, not the coordination number.

This is the "three true + one invented" P1 shape. Item 4 sounds plausible but the well's
*position* is a length scale; coordination number comes from the lattice geometry (Ch. 2).

questions.reason: Added thermal energy raises the average atom up the shallower *attractive* wall of the energy well more than the steep repulsive one, so the time-averaged spacing exceeds *r₀*.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: d
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true; the asymmetry explanation is precisely why thermal expansion occurs.
questions.concise: The well's asymmetry (shallower attractive wall) raises the mean spacing on heating.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: solids expand when heated.
- R is TRUE: the attractive wall of the energy well is shallower than the steep repulsive wall.
Added thermal energy lifts atoms higher up the well; because of the asymmetry, the extra space
gained on the attractive side exceeds the space lost on the repulsive side, so the *time-averaged*
spacing rises above r₀.

This is worth internalising because the naive picture ("heating = faster vibration = bigger
orbit") is not the real mechanism — the *shape* of the well is. Expect this to appear again.

questions.text: Given E(r) = −A/rᵐ + B/rⁿ, the condition that fixes the equilibrium spacing *r₀* is:
questions.keyExplanation: Setting dE/dr = 0 and solving gives *r₀*.
questions.concise: Equilibrium is where the energy curve has zero slope (its minimum).
questions.detailed: The equilibrium spacing r₀ is at the minimum of E(r), so dE/dr = 0 at r = r₀. **(d)** is correct. Option (a), d²E/dr² = 0, is not the minimum condition; (b), E = 0, is not the equilibrium binding energy; and (c) is not a meaningful derivative condition.

questions.text: In E(r) = −A/rᵐ + B/rⁿ, the exponent relationship required is:
questions.keyExplanation: n > m makes the repulsive term rise more steeply as r → 0.
questions.concise: n > m makes the repulsive term rise more steeply as r → 0.
questions.detailed:
In E(r) = −A/rᵐ + B/rⁿ:
- The attractive term −A/rᵐ dominates at large r.
- The repulsive term +B/rⁿ dominates at small r.
For repulsion to win as r → 0 (which physically it must — atoms cannot overlap), we need
**n > m**. Typical ionic values quoted are m = 1, n = 9.

questions.text: A material has a deep, narrow interatomic potential-energy well around its equilibrium spacing $r_0$. Which statements are expected?

statements.text: A deeper well generally indicates stronger cohesive bonding and a higher melting temperature.
A narrow well has high curvature near equilibrium and is associated with a high elastic modulus.
A narrow, deep well is generally associated with a relatively low thermal expansion coefficient.
The narrow well means atoms can move far from $r_0$ under a small stress because the restoring force is weak.

questions.keyExplanation: Statements 1–3 follow the usual potential-well interpretation. Statement 4 reverses the curvature argument: a narrow well has a steep local restoring response, not a weak one.
questions.concise: Well depth relates to cohesive energy; curvature relates to stiffness and helps explain the expansion trend.
questions.detailed: A deeper potential well indicates greater cohesive energy, while a narrower well means the potential changes rapidly with displacement near equilibrium. The curvature at the minimum is related to elastic stiffness. Thermal expansion also depends on anharmonicity, so the well picture is a qualitative trend rather than a universal numerical rule. Statement 4 incorrectly associates a narrow well with weak restoring forces.

questions.text: At the equilibrium spacing *r₀*, the attractive and repulsive forces are both individually zero.

options.label: b
options.text: False — their *sum* is zero, but each is finite

questions.keyExplanation: Each force is finite and non-zero; only their *sum* vanishes.
questions.concise: At r₀ the attractive and repulsive forces are individually non-zero; only the resultant vanishes.
questions.detailed:
At r₀:
```
F_attractive + F_repulsive = 0   (net force zero)
```
but neither term is zero individually — they exactly cancel. If either were zero, a small
displacement would not be resisted and the solid would have no stiffness. This is why r₀ is a
*genuine* equilibrium with restoring forces on both sides, not a "force-free" point.

questions.text: Choose the statement(s) that correctly connect the interatomic energy curve to engineering properties.

statements.text: The curvature of the well at *r₀* sets the elastic modulus.
The asymmetry of the well causes thermal expansion.
The depth of the well correlates with melting point.
The width of the well at half-depth determines the coordination number.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is invented — the well does not set coordination number. [P3]
questions.concise: Curvature→modulus, asymmetry→expansion, depth→melting; well width does not set coordination number.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: curvature of the well at r₀ sets the elastic modulus.
- Item 2 — TRUE: asymmetry causes thermal expansion.
- Item 3 — TRUE: well depth correlates with melting point.
- Item 4 — FALSE: the "width at half-depth" is not what determines coordination number; the
  coordination number comes from the crystal structure (Ch. 2), not the energy-well shape.

Note the P3 angle: all three valid links are about *bonding (potential) energy* and the shape
of the energy curve — none of them is about heat as thermal energy.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about bond *directionality* is/are correct?

statements.text: The ionic bond is non-directional — an ion is attracted by counter-ions equally in every direction.
The covalent bond is strongly directional — it points along fixed atomic orbitals.
The metallic bond is non-directional because the conduction electrons are delocalised.
van der Waals bonding is a *primary* bond and is stronger than covalent bonding for exactly that reason.

questions.keyExplanation: Ionic and metallic bonds are non-directional; covalent is directional. van der Waals is secondary and weak, so item 4 is false. [P2]
questions.concise: Ionic and metallic bonds are non-directional and covalent is directional; van der Waals is weak and secondary, so item 4 is false.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: the ionic bond is electrostatic and acts equally in all directions around an ion. **TRUE**
- Item 2 — TRUE: covalent bonding uses fixed orbital overlap, so it is strongly directional. **TRUE**
- Item 3 — TRUE: the metallic "electron sea" is delocalised, so no fixed bond direction exists. **TRUE**
- Item 4 — FALSE: van der Waals bonding is a *secondary* bond of 1–10 kJ/mol, weaker than any primary bond. **FALSE**

Ionic and metallic bonding are both non-directional, which is why both permit close packing of
atoms (Ch. 2). Covalent directionality is what imposes low-coordination structures such as diamond
and ice.
**Trap check:** item 4 sounds authoritative because it names a real property (directionality) —
but attaches the wrong strength claim. Check the *energy class* before accepting a bond comparison.

questions.text: In graphite, the carbon atoms within a single layer are held together by ______ bonds, and the separate layers are held to one another by ______.
questions.keyExplanation: Strong covalent bonding within each layer; only weak van der Waals between layers — hence graphite is a soft lubricant.
questions.concise: Giant covalent *layers* plus weak van der Waals between them → graphite is soft and slippery.
questions.detailed: Within each graphite layer, carbon atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds; adjacent layers are held together by weak van der Waals forces. **(c)** is correct. The other options reverse or misidentify these bonding types.

questions.assertion: Materials with larger bond energies typically show both higher melting points and higher elastic moduli.
questions.reason: Melting and elastic straining both require changing the interatomic spacing against the cohesive force, and a deeper energy well means more energy must be supplied to do so.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R is **not** the correct explanation

options.label: c
options.text: Both A and R true, R is the correct explanation of A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true: melting and straining both fight the same cohesive bond, and well depth sets its strength.
questions.concise: Both true — melting and straining both fight the cohesive bond, so a deeper well gives a higher melting point and a higher modulus.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: materials with large bonding energies (W, diamond, Al₂O₃) also show high melting
  points and high elastic moduli. This is a well-established trend, not a coincidence.
- R is TRUE: melting means pulling the atoms apart against the cohesive attraction; elastic
  straining means displacing them against the restoring force. Both are governed by the same
  interatomic energy well.
A deeper well (larger E₀) therefore means more thermal energy is needed to melt the solid *and* a
steeper restoring force on displacement — so R explains why A holds.

questions.text: The maximum number of electrons that a subshell with azimuthal quantum number *l* = 3 can accommodate is:
questions.keyExplanation: 2(2l + 1) = 2(7) = 14 — the f subshell holds 7 orbitals.
questions.concise: 2(2l + 1) = 2(7) = 14 for the f subshell (l = 3).
questions.detailed: For l = 3, the subshell is f and contains 2l + 1 = 7 orbitals, each holding two electrons: 14 electrons. **(b)** is correct. Option (a) is the capacity of one orbital; (c) is an eight-electron value; and (d) is the n = 4 shell capacity, not a subshell capacity.

questions.text: Which statements describe secondary (van der Waals-type) bonding?

statements.text: It arises from permanent, fluctuating or induced electric dipoles.
Its typical energy scale is much lower than that of primary metallic, ionic or covalent bonds.
Hydrogen bonding is commonly treated as a relatively strong special case of secondary bonding.
Secondary bonding is the main cohesive force throughout diamond’s three-dimensional carbon network.

questions.keyExplanation: Statements 1–3 describe secondary bonding. Statement 4 is false: diamond’s three-dimensional network is held together by strong covalent bonds.
questions.concise: Secondary bonding comes from dipoles and is much weaker than the covalent network holding diamond together.
questions.detailed: Van der Waals interactions arise from permanent or induced dipoles and are much weaker than primary bonds. Hydrogen bonding is often taught as a stronger special case of secondary interaction. Diamond’s rigidity and high melting temperature arise from its extended covalent network, not from van der Waals forces.
